title: Fact-check: Pakistani flags at Dhruv Rathee's anti-Modi protest in London?
description: The video does not show Dhruv Rathee’s protest in London Updated Thursday Oct 22 2026 Social media posts claim that a video showing Pakistani and Bangladeshi flags was filmed at a London protest organised by Indian influencer and activist Dhruv Rathee against the Indian government and in support of the youth protests in India. The claim is false. The footage is actually from an August gathering in London celebrating Indian and Pakistani Independence Day. On October 18, users on X, formerly known as Twitter, shared a 46-second video clip claiming to show Pakistani and Bangladeshi flags at a protest organised by Indian social media influencer and activist Dhruv Rathee in London. “This raises serious questions about the forces rallying behind this campaign and the narrative being pushed,” one post read. “This is no longer about the BJP or PM Modi. This is about India.” The post implied that Pakistan and Bangladesh were supporting, and possibly organising, protests against the government of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. At the time of writing, the video had garnered 51,900 views, 1,000 likes and 595 reposts. Similar claims have also been shared on Instagram and elsewhere on X . The video does not show Dhruv Rathee’s protest in London, held on October 17. Instead, the footage is from an open-air gathering in London on August 15, 2026, where British Pakistani singer Amir Hashmi performed at an event celebrating the independence of Pakistan and India. Hashmi shared additional videos from the gathering on his Instagram account, explaining that he organises the event annually to bring Indians and Pakistanis together. “Every year on August 15, I bring Pakistanis and Indians together in London to celebrate peace, unity and humanity,” he wrote, “Pakistanis singing the Indian national anthem, and Indians singing the Pakistani national anthem, standing together with love and respect.” His post can be viewed here . Hashmi also confirmed to Geo Fact Check in messages that the video was recorded on August 15, 2026. “This video was recorded on August 15, when I brought Indians and Pakistanis together to promote unity, mutual respect, and peace,” Hashmi said. “I do this every year, encouraging both communities to respect each other’s national flags and anthems.” Murtaza Ali Shah, Geo News correspondent in the United Kingdom, also told Geo Fact Check over the phone that the footage was unrelated to Rathee’s protest. “This is an old video. This video has absolutely nothing to do with Dhruv Rathee’s protest in London. The claim in it is fake,” Shah said. He added that no Pakistani flags were visible at Rathee’s protest and that Rathee held one event in London, outside Parliament Square. Video of the protest can be viewed here. Verdict: The video does not show Dhruv Rathee’s protest in London. It was recorded on August 15, 2026, at a public gathering where British Pakistani singer Amir Hashmi brought Indians and Pakistanis together to promote peace and unity. Follow us on @GeoFactCheck on X (Twitter) and @geo_factcheck on Instagram. If our readers detect any errors, we encourage them to contact us at [email protected]

title: Emergency or overreach?
description: Published October 21, 2026 As a matter of course, every constitution and international treaty that confers rights and obligations on the parties presupposes a stable environment for smooth operation. Paradoxically, however, change is the only permanent feature of the world we live in. Aware of this basic truth, the framers of constitutions and treaties incorporate ‘exception’ clauses into the legal documents they draw up. Such provisions aim to allow a temporary departure from some guaranteed rights or stipulated obligations if an abnormal situation arises. The same may apply to the recent presidential proclamation of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP). Federalism or provincial autonomy is a cardinal principle of the 1973 constitution. Executive, financial and legislative powers are distributed between the federation or the federal government on one hand and the provinces on the other. In the normal course of events, the federal government can’t interfere with constitutionally mandated provincial autonomy, except in a few instances. Article 148 (1), for example, stipulates that “The executive authority of every province shall be so exercised as to secure compliance with Federal laws which apply in that province”. Clause (2) of the same article states: “It shall be the duty of the federation to protect every province against external aggression and internal disturbances and to ensure that the government of every province is carried on in accordance with the provisions of the constitution”. Likewise, Article 149 confers on the federal government the power to issue directions to the provinces to “ensure that executive authority of a province is exercised as not to impede exercise of the executive authority of the federation” and to “prevent any grave menace to the peace or tranquility or economic life of Pakistan” or any part of the country. It follows that even in normal circumstances, the federal government is constitutionally mandated to protect the people of a province against both external aggression and internal disturbances. Leaving aside the phrase ‘external aggression’, the phrase ‘internal disturbances’ hasn’t been qualified by an adjective, such as ‘material’ or ‘grave’ or ‘serious’. This means that if we go by the text of the relevant provisions of the constitution, the federal government’s mandate is triggered by any level of internal disturbance in a province. The federal government is mandated not only to ensure that provinces are constitutionally governed, but also that they don’t deviate from the constitution. Both these obligations are perpetual and don’t need any upheavals to exercise them. Arising from the federal government’s dual mandate – protecting the provinces and ensuring constitutional governance therein – is the power to issue directions to the federating units on how they exercise their executive authority. For their part, the provinces must obey all federal laws. It’s understood that compliance with a law includes compliance with the policies and executive orders made under it. The emergency powers of the president and the federal government primarily emanate from Articles 148 and 149. The constitution provides for three kinds of emergencies: national emergency (under Article 232), constitutional emergency (under Article 234), and financial emergency (under Article 235). The president has invoked Articles 232 and 234 to clamp an emergency and the governor’s rule on KP. So, we’ll leave aside the provisions relating to financial emergency. Article 232 states: “If the president is satisfied that a grave emergency exists in which the security of Pakistan, or any part thereof, is threatened by war or external aggression, or by internal disturbance beyond the power of a provincial government to control, he may issue a Proclamation of Emergency”. The concisely framed text sets out two conditions for imposing a national emergency: the threat to the country’s, or a part of the country’s, security must be grave enough, and the situation must be beyond a province’s capacity to respond effectively. If either condition isn’t met, the proclamation of emergency is unwarranted. Article 233 empowers the federal government to suspend fundamental rights while a national emergency proclamation is in force. Such a situation arose in 1998 when a nationwide emergency was proclaimed following Pakistan’s nuclear tests. The Supreme Court upheld the proclamation. Article 234 provides that “If the president, on receipt of a report from the governor of a province, is satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the government of the province cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the constitution”, he may clamp emergency on that province. Here, again, two conditions are stipulated: a constitutional breakdown in a province, and that the provincial governor, as a representative of the federation, has apprised the president of it. Per the notification issued by the federal government, all the relevant conditions for clamping emergency and the governor’s rule on KP were met: One, there has been an ‘alarming increase’ in acts of terrorism and violence in the province. Two, the provincial government ‘failed’ to effectively respond to those acts. Third, the KP governor reported a ‘constitutional breakdown’ in the province. The opposition, which ruled KP before the imposition of the emergency, has contested these claims, describing the proclamation as politically motivated and pre-planned and arguing that, instead of addressing the security situation, it would aggravate it. Thus, the question involved here is not primarily a question of law, as the federal government indisputably commands emergency powers, but a question of fact: whether the situation in KP had deteriorated to such an extent as to warrant intervention from Islamabad. It may be argued that the federal government’s executive powers in provinces in normal circumstances (Articles 148-149) and the emergency powers that arise out of those powers run counter to the principle of provincial autonomy. Be that as it may, the 18th Amendment, which shored up provincial autonomy and was enacted in 2010 with the consensus of almost all political parties, didn’t do away with those federal powers. This may be interpreted to mean that, in principle, political parties agree on such powers. The question is when to exercise that authority. title: China bets on manufactured water, and wants to sell it to the world
description:
Published October 22, 2026 China is emerging as a major supplier of water technology to parched countries across Asia, the Middle East and Africa, as shrinking natural supplies at home push Beijing to invest heavily in manufactured freshwater, industry experts say. Chinese firms are selling desalination membranes, filtration equipment and engineering services to Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, often through the Belt and Road Initiative, which connects Chinese capital and infrastructure projects to developing markets. Even Gulf states, long desalination pioneers, are turning to Chinese manufacturers to produce equipment at scale. China exported more than $2 billion of water filtering and purifying machinery in 2025, up 25% from $1.6 billion in 2020, according to UN Comtrade. Vontron Technology said it shipped more than 30,000 seawater desalination membranes to Belt and Road countries last year, enough for more than 300,000 tons of daily capacity. In January, PowerChina said it was building a water supply project in Tanzania to serve more than 450,000 people. At home, Beijing has made water security a strategic priority. Spending on water conservancy has grown faster than military spending since 2015, according to China Water Risk (CWR), a Hong Kong-based think tank. It now exceeds 1.2 trillion yuan ($170 billion) a year, which CWR says rivals China's central military budget. The push is rooted in domestic risk. In August, a glacier collapse near the border between Nepal and Tibet showed how volatile natural water sources are becoming. Tibet's "water towers" feed headwaters for nearly two billion people across South, Southeast and East Asia, and climate change is eroding them. Meanwhile, severe over-extraction in northern China has depleted groundwater and left key farming regions with systemic deficits. "We could see peak water by 2050 across 10 major river systems that provide water to one in two Asians as glacier melt peaks and river flows decline," CWR said. Peak water is the tipping point where flows from natural water sources reach a maximum and thereafter enter continual decline. "This will put almost half the GDP of 16 countries at risk, including China,” CWR said. Benjamin Horton, dean of the School of Energy and Environment at City University of Hong Kong, said China's ability to develop water technology at scale could cut costs for other water-stressed countries. He said Beijing could become Asia's leading provider of practical water security solutions. "Through the Belt and Road Initiative, there is likely to be continued demand for hydropower, desalination, flood forecasting, irrigation, wastewater treatment, and climate-resilient infrastructure," he said. In July, China rolled out new regulations under its Five-Year Plan that treat water as a pillar of national security and economic self-reliance, not just an environmental issue. Surface water supplies about 80% of China's freshwater, while recycled water, desalinated seawater and harvested rainwater provide just 3% to 4%. Authorities have pledged to raise that share. The South-North Water Transfer Project moves billions of cubic meters from the Yangtze to the dry north, but it is constrained by energy costs and shrinking surpluses in the warming Yangtze basin. Saleh Al Khabti, China president of Saudi developer Acwa, said costs are rising and quality is deteriorating in some areas. China operated 167 seawater desalination projects at the end of 2025, with total capacity of 3,076,805 tons a day, up 221,283 tons from 2024, according to the Ministry of Natural Resources. State media put the average production cost at 4 to 8 yuan per cubic meter. Industry reports expect the market to grow from $1.84 billion in 2024 to $4.66 billion in 2033, or about 11% a year. Hurdles remain, including the scale of investment and the central planning needed for multi-city conveyance grids, while public attitudes also pose a challenge. Khabti said many Chinese still view drinking desalinated water as taboo, though local governments are keen to build capacity. Khabti said more than 90% of the renewable equipment Acwa procures comes from Chinese manufacturers, and the company buys about 70% of its global water equipment from Chinese suppliers. Acwa has pledged to invest up to $30 billion in China by 2030, working with firms including PowerChina and China Energy Engineering Corporation. It plans to spend at least $15 billion a year on Chinese equipment over the next three years across renewables, green hydrogen and desalination. Khabti expects Chinese membrane makers to catch up fast. "It took us 15 years to reach where we are today with our partners," he said. He thinks Chinese original equipment manufacturers could match that level in two to three years, and he expects desalination to follow wind and solar as "a big area of exports." "We're very bullish about China," he said. "Once it's there, China will be the leader." Copyright © 2026. Geo Television Network. All Rights Reserved.

title: A 'misunderstood' relationship?
description: Published October 22, 2026 The subject of the US-Pakistan relationship is inexhaustible. It is perhaps the most talked-about, but arguably the least understood, relationship. We keep writing about it and finding new meanings. I, for one, am still learning. This article is not a history of the relationship, a review of its current state or a look into the future. It is a series of personal observations on how the two governments have conducted the relationship, explained it to the public and how the public perceived it in the past. This is certainly not the last word on the subject. Just one person’s observations, for what they are worth. Pakistan has remained relevant, if not important, to US interests in South Asia for one reason or another ever since the two countries began their on-again, off-again alliance in the early fifties. The alliance provided Pakistan with invaluable help in its early years to stabilise, build a platform for economic development, and strengthen its defence capability. But this was the last time the US really helped Pakistan. In subsequent decades, Washington engaged primarily with the government, which happened to be military or military-dominated. And the relationship was war-related. While the ruling establishment benefited, Pakistan’s gain was doubtful. Arguably, the country lost more than it gained from the American connection, even though it involved significant economic aid and security assistance. America’s failing wars always leave behind consequences for its partners which no amount of aid can compensate. One reason the relationship challenges average understanding is American domestic politics. If the US had pursued such an extraordinary aid relationship with Pakistan from time to time, where it saw no lasting economic or strategic interests, then more than a critical foreign policy issue was at play. The specific task given to Pakistan was important not only strategically but also politically, especially during the 80s Afghan war, the post 9/11 Afghanistan war and the ‘war on terror’. Domestic politics always weighs heavily on wars. This has been especially true in America, where wars have always had many stakeholders and served many interests. The poorly informed general public, which influenced electoral politics, looked for victory in the wars and the allies’ submission to US demands and interests, even at the cost of their own national interest. Because of all that, Pakistan, which was an important partner in these wars, came to be handled by the successive administrations in the US through a relationship that was far out of proportion to the country’s normal importance. Given the nature of the relationship, focusing largely on military intelligence cooperation and its importance to American electoral politics, the White House drove it, aided by the Pentagon and the CIA. So the relationship had an underworld the two sides could not discuss openly. You could talk about the differences but not the cooperation, at least not the full extent of it. Ironically, America’s failure often made even valuable cooperation from an ally inconsequential. The same calculus applied on the Pakistan side, where even valuable help from Washington was often inconsequential because of the country’s poor governance. So the public in both countries focused only on the negatives. This was another reason why the relationship was not fully understood. The relationship operated at several levels, and it has been riddled with contradictions. It was not a strategic relationship, but ironically, it was never truly transactional either. It was transactional, but it dealt with strategic issues, some of which were contentious. The two countries’ interests did not always coincide. Pakistan’s own poor policy choices, especially the support for the Taliban, also contributed to its misfortunes. Pakistan cannot only blame Washington. Pakistan, however, became addicted to US economic support and strategic patronage, and the relationship became a birthmark of its foreign policy. Islamabad convinced itself that, given its geopolitical location, it was of fixed, unchanging importance to Washington. Pakistan wanted a strategic relationship, but with no strategic reason for a long-term commitment to Pakistan, the US could not stay in the relationship for long and exited as soon as its needs were met. Washington needed Islamabad’s cooperation in the short term to serve its critical security and strategic interests, while Pakistan needed long-term US support. Not only that, their policies, perceptions and interests contradicted each other, as did their relations with other countries. Neither side understood this dilemma; their needs were only partially met and their expectations largely unfulfilled, setting them up for disappointment and cries of betrayal. Other contradictions also marked the relationship. In Pakistan, successive governments made the relationship with the US part of Pakistan’s organising idea, giving Washington the impression that the country, especially its political leadership, could not survive without American help. And in times of dire need, Washington overindulged Pakistan, which left a lingering feeling among the establishment that the US cannot walk away from Pakistan. The US did not share Pakistan’s expectations for the relationship and did not want to commit to it long term, especially against India. But through hyperbole, a hallmark of US public policy, and agreements that offered vague commitments, Washington kept Pakistan under the illusion of a strategic alliance, because it did not want to lose its support. In time, Pakistan discovered the reality. Pakistan too misrepresented its policies to satisfy Washington, as it did not want to lose American support. The truth is, neither side was honest with the other. The Pakistan government, especially a military one, had to remain mindful not to go entirely against public sentiment. It tried to maintain a careful balance between meeting US demands and accommodating public pressure. But Washington kept upsetting that balance by demanding more from Pakistan. As the government got squeezed between America’s demand to do more and public pressure to do less, it sometimes ended up supporting the US with half-hearted, weak policies that satisfied neither Washington nor the Pakistani public. This contributed to the tensions in the relationship. As for the future: it has been a need-based relationship in which Pakistan qualified for...

title: Australian fast bowler Megan Schutt suspended over medication breach
description:
Published October 22, 2026 Star Australian fast bowler Megan Schutt was suspended for two matches on Thursday for breaching prescription medication rules. The 33-year-old, who was a standout in Australia's recent one-day series against Bangladesh, apologised for "failing to meet the standards" expected of her. Cricket Australia said in a statement she breached "requirements under the Sports Science and Sports Medicine guidelines with regard to prescription medication". "This relates to a single incident which occurred while out of competition and was not for performance-enhancing purposes," it added. "We will continue to provide appropriate support to Megan and reinforce the standards and responsibilities expected of everyone representing our game." Her two-match ban will see Schutt miss on Thursday's third and final T20 against New Zealand and the Adelaide Strikers' opening game of the Women's Big Bash League later this month. "I fully accept the penalty handed down and apologise for failing to meet the standards expected of me," said Schutt, who has played 114 ODIs and 126 T20s for Australia. "I'm sorry for the attention this has caused and appreciate the support I've received." Copyright © 2026. Geo Television Network. All Rights Reserved.

title: Encounters of the deadly kind
description: Published October 23, 2026 In less than 48 hours this week, two men at the centre of high-profile cases died at the hands of apparent police ‘crossfire’, and the police gave the same explanation both times. In Islamabad, Muhammad Nauman, accused in the case linked to the suicide of student Laiba Ejaz, was allegedly hit by his own accomplices’ fire while police were taking him to recover evidence. No policeman was hurt, though. A day later, Tauqeer Nazir, prime suspect in the killing of orphaned teenager Waseem Abbas in Multan, died in a CCD encounter near Bahawalpur, allegedly from his accomplice’s gunfire. He had escaped from Multan’s DHA police station while on a four-day physical remand. No explanation is available for how he escaped and reached Bahawalpur. Meanwhile, the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) documented at least 670 CCD-led encounters in eight months of 2025, in which 924 suspects died, and only two police officers were killed. The HRCP’s report for 2024 recorded 341 encounter deaths across Punjab and Sindh combined for the entire year. The police story rarely changes: Suspects’ accomplices ambush the police party to free them, the police fire back, and the suspect is killed by their own accomplices’ bullets, while they always escape unhurt. In October 2025, Islamabad police gave a near-identical account when two suspects in the murder of CDA Director Land Ehsan Elahi were found dead after their accomplices allegedly opened fire. When the same improbable event happens hundreds of times, the story stops being probable. Several factors drive this trend. The first cause is structural. Investigation is weak, forensic capacity is thin, witnesses are intimidated, prosecution is under-resourced and trials drag on for years. The encounter has become a shortcut around a justice system the state has failed to repair. The second is political ownership. The CCD was created in 2025 through an ordinance amending the Police Order 2002, and Punjab’s leadership has hailed it as protecting citizens’ lives and property. Rana Sanaullah has defended it on the grounds that those killed were proclaimed offenders who did not submit to the law. When politicians condone extrajudicial outcomes and ignore process, policemen learn what is expected of them. The third is the outrage economy. In the Laiba case, the prime minister directed Islamabad’s police chief to ensure immediate arrest. In Multan, CCTV footage of the boy being run over circulated widely. Under that kind of pressure, only a dead suspect is counted as service delivery. Another thing is about impunity. Punjab police’s own figures recorded 2,246 suspects killed in 3,424 encounters between 1990 and mid-2005. None of these cases produced a lasting deterrent, so each new one carries little fear for those who pull the trigger. Unsurprisingly, authorities apply the encounter approach selectively to suspects without money, connections or influential surnames. In Karachi’s Karsaz case, the accused was acquitted after an out-of-court settlement. The Shahzeb Khan murder case ended the same way, with Shahrukh Jatoi’s acquittal in 2023. The street learns a simple lesson: poor suspects are shot on some bypass road at night, while privileged ones walk free through legal compromises. Two legal systems, divided by class, damage the state’s credibility more than any gang. That these encounters give victims justice is an outright farce. What victims actually get is raw retribution, without fairness, evidence or remedy. Police sources say Laiba gave Nauman Rs2.1 million, raised from the sale of her father’s plot, along with her stepmother’s jewellery, and they suspect he defrauded other women. A due trial and thorough investigation could have traced the money, identified the racket and other victims, and led to court-ordered restitution and compensation to victims’ heirs. The family has lost a daughter and its savings, and the state has closed off the only legal route to recovering them. Even if Nauman was guilty, fraud carries a prison sentence, not death. Yet he ended up dead in police custody, and a society that cheers such deaths shares the blame. Max Weber defined the state by its claim to a legitimate monopoly on violence. That violence is legitimate because it is bound by law and answerable to courts. Once police decide who dies by the roadside, the state becomes just the best-armed actor in a crowded field. Each staged encounter also deepens legal cynicism, the belief that law serves power. It teaches young people that brute force settles disputes and lends legitimacy to private revenge and jirga justice. Unchecked power over life and death also becomes a source of unrestricted coercion. The HRCP recorded one family’s account of police pressure to bury the deceased immediately, with a warning that other relatives could be killed if they pursued the case. When citizens fear the thana rather than trust it, they stop reporting crime and witnesses stop cooperating. Investigation weakens, which produces more encounters. Officers who can close cases with a gun have no reason to develop investigative skill. Tauqeer died under a court-ordered remand, which turned the magistrate’s protection into a joke. Has the crime declined? The Punjab Police reports that in 2025, compared with 2024, robbery and dacoity fell by 71 per cent, murder during robbery by 73 per cent and overall murder by 23 per cent. No independent audit or victimisation survey has verified this. Then, the picture is uneven: motorcycle theft, the crime that hurts ordinary citizens most, continued to rise, with over 75,000 thefts recorded in 2025, and crimes against women grew as a share of registered cases in the first half of 2026. Lastly, correlation is not causation. More patrolling, faster response, and better surveillance may explain much of the decline, and criminology consistently finds that the certainty of being caught deters more than the severity of punishment. A more lasting decline in crime needs a different set of measures. For instance, every custodial or encounter death should trigger a mandatory, time-bound judicial inquiry under relevant sections of the CrPC, with the findings published. The custody transfers need safeguards: body cameras, GPS-tracked vehicles, prior...

title: Harry Brook's 202 sets new record for highest ODI score in Pakistan
description:
Published October 22, 2026 England captain Harry Brook delivered a breathtaking performance, smashing 202 runs off 116 balls, including 21 fours and 10 sixes, to guide his side to an imposing total of 429-4 in 50 overs. Brook's double century set a new record for the highest individual score in a men’s ODI innings played in Pakistan. He eclipsed the previous benchmark of 188 runs, set by former South Africa captain Gary Kirsten against the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in Rawalpindi in 1996. The England skipper’s remarkable innings also saw him rewrite several other records. Brook also set a new record for the highest individual score by an England batter in men's ODIs, eclipsing former captain Ben Stokes' 182 against New Zealand in 2023. Furthermore, his double century came off just 116 balls, making it the fastest ODI double century by balls faced, surpassing India's Shubman Gill, who scored an unbeaten 223 off 117 deliveries against the West Indies in Guwahati on 30 September 2026. The 27-year-old also joined an elite group of captains to have scored double centuries in men's ODIs. His innings ranks among the highest individual scores by a captain in the format and makes him the first England captain to register an ODI double century.  Copyright © 2026. Geo Television Network. title: Punjab CM directs enforcement of ban on smart glasses, other spy devices
description:
Published October 22, 2026 LAHORE: Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz has directed authorities to ensure a ban on camera-equipped glasses and other spy devices across the province, amid complaints regarding illegal surveillance through spying devices. The directions come days after the provincial government decided to impose a ban on devices used for spying, including glasses, pens, watches and other gadgets equipped with hidden cameras and recording equipment. A Punjab Home Department spokesperson had said that strict legal action would be taken against the use, purchase and sale of spying equipment and concealed electronic devices, according to The News . The decision has been taken to protect citizens' privacy and personal information, particularly to ensure the safety of women and children, the spokesperson added. According to the spokesperson, complaints have emerged regarding illegal surveillance, harassment and blackmail through the use of spying devices. The spokesperson maintained that the Punjab government was committed to protecting citizens' fundamental rights, personal information and privacy. Strict punishment would be imposed for the illegal use of everyday items equipped with hidden cameras, the spokesperson said. The move comes amid growing global calls for action against "pervert" smart glasses after secretly filmed footage of girls and women appeared online— with a petition in Britain demanding a ban on their sale. Anyone wearing smart glasses can take photos, film videos, listen to music, make phone calls, translate text or interact with an AI assistant, with sales now hitting the millions, according to AFP . The devices grabbed attention this summer after a marketing tie-up between Kylie Jenner, beauty mogul and member of the Kardashian dynasty, and tech giant Meta. Worries reached a peak in the summer in Europe, especially in Britain which saw intense media coverage of so-called "pervert glasses" alongisde reports that Meta is developing a facial recognition feature to be integrated into the devices. In one case, a 17-year-old girl told British broadcaster Channel 4 News in August how she had been approached by a man who covertly recorded her and their interaction. Norway's capital Oslo banned the glasses in schools, while France's CNIL data protection watchdog urged "vigilance". Copyright © 2026. Geo Television Network. All Rights Reserved.

title: The future of money, AI and the state
description: Published October 20, 2026 I returned from two days at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok with a clear conviction: the future of finance is becoming inseparable from the state’s capacity. Debt, inflation, fiscal discipline and investment remain essential. But the programme also addresses tokenisation, agentic AI, digital infrastructure and AI’s potential to create jobs. Increasingly, these are parts of the same economic agenda. I met World Bank Vice President and Treasurer Jorge Familiar; IFC Regional Vice President Imad Fakhoury; World Bank Vice President for Digital & AI Sangbu Kim; and World Bank Group Controller Zinga Venner. We discussed digital capital markets, investment, AI-enabled regulation and blockchain-based financial transparency. We entered those conversations with progress behind us. Pakistan has established a statutory framework for virtual assets, introduced regulatory application routes and enabled conditional banking access for licensed providers. Now we must build an environment where enterprise grows, investors have confidence and people participate with meaningful protection. Three questions stand out: How can innovation help businesses access capital? How can regulators supervise increasingly complex markets? And how can governments know where public money goes? On October 8, the IMF published analysis drawing on its Global Financial Stability Report chapter on tokenisation. Its assessment was neither unqualified enthusiasm nor blanket rejection: markets remain small and fragmented, constrained by legal uncertainty, interoperability and settlement. Tokenisation connects issuance, trading, settlement and servicing through programmable ledgers. But greater speed can accelerate financial stress. The IMF emphasises enforceable rights, consistent regulation and safe settlement assets. Pakistan must participate in this conversation. The question is not whether an asset can be tokenised, but whether holders have enforceable claims and the system works when something goes wrong. The IMF’s New Economy Forum paired tokenisation with agentic AI. As assets become programmable and software acts on delegated instructions, who authorises actions, sets limits and remains accountable? Regulatory capability must develop alongside technology, not after markets have scaled. In 2024, the World Bank issued a CHF200 million digital bond, using Swiss National Bank wholesale central bank digital currency for settlement, while preserving familiar custody channels. In June 2025, IFC invested $100 million in Isbank’s digitally native note in Türkiye. Settled the same day through Euroclear’s digital infrastructure, its proceeds were intended for businesses, farmers and entrepreneurs in earthquake-affected provinces. These are earlier precedents, but they explain why engagement with Treasury and IFC matters. For Pakistan, could a digital bond or sukuk improve settlement or investor access? Would investors buy it? Can custodians hold it? Are full costs lower, including legal and operational expenses? Digitising debt does not make the borrower more creditworthy. Cheaper processing does not automatically mean cheaper borrowing. The objective should be better financing, with technology serving that objective. My discussion with the World Bank Controller included blockchain-enabled financial transparency. The World Bank’s FundsChain platform helps stakeholders trace development funds and connect transactions with supporting records. In July 2026, the Bank reported that its original platform had expanded to more than 300 projects across more than 90 countries. Ethiopia’s FundsChain Evolution pilot goes further, exploring conditions embedded directly into payment flows. Tracking money asks: Where did the funds go? Programmable controls ask: Can a payment occur only when specified conditions are met? Governments could explore this for development spending, subject to legal authority, privacy and exceptions. A blockchain does not eliminate the need for auditors or physical verification. An immutable record can preserve incorrect information, and recording a payment does not prove that a service was delivered. A digital audit trail is valuable. It is not an audit verdict. But connecting authorisation, payment, documentation and oversight more effectively deserves serious examination. On October 14, the IMF and World Bank Group released the Bangkok Blueprint, developed with the Bank of Thailand to address cyber-enabled fraud in digital financial services. Its 12 key considerations across five pillars cover legal foundations, prevention, enforcement, cooperation and consumer protection. Fraud crosses financial institutions and digital platforms, demanding coordination. For Pakistan, innovation cannot be measured only by how quickly money moves. We must ask how quickly institutions identify scams, share information lawfully, respond and help affected customers. Faster payments are not progress for someone whose savings reach a fraudster faster. At PVARA, innovation and supervision must advance together, with accountable providers and effective safeguards. Trust is not a public-relations benefit of good regulation. It is a condition that allows financial markets to grow. Its October economic update for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan estimated that AI could significantly augment 13-20% of jobs, while fewer than 10% face near-term automation risk. These regional estimates are potential, not guaranteed productivity gains for Pakistan. The report identifies gaps in local relevance and productive adoption. Urdu accounts for around 0.03% of URLs in the cited Common Crawl dataset, illustrating why local context matters, even though it doesn’t represent all AI training data. Pakistan should avoid reducing AI policy to announcing the largest model or purchasing the most equipment. At PVARA, I want to pursue AI-assisted regulatory work: retrieving relevant laws, identifying missing application information, supporting supervisory analysis and preserving institutional knowledge securely. The aim is not to transfer public authority to an algorithm. It is to give accountable officials better tools. Data-centre investments demand reliable power, connectivity, cooling, customers and commercial viability. Available electricity alone is not an investment proposition. The objective is not simply to own more technology. The objective is to generate more economic value from it. title: 13-year-old Karachi girl rescued after receiving dangerous online tasks
description:
Published October 23, 2026     KARACHI: The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) has rescued a 13-year-old girl in Karachi from a suspected dark web-linked network that allegedly instructed her to poison a cat before ordering her to seriously harm herself, officials said. The NCCIA intervention followed intelligence shared by an international agency, which alerted Pakistani authorities to suspicious online activity and provided internet protocol (IP) addresses linked to the network. According to NCCIA officials, the girl had become involved with an online group that assigned her dangerous tasks. As part of the first task, she was allegedly ordered to poison a cat, resulting in its death. The second task involved instructions to inflict serious harm on herself. However, NCCIA investigators managed to locate the girl before she could carry out the second instruction. Officials said the international agency had provided IP addresses being used from 13 countries, including Pakistan. The NCCIA's Karachi team conducted a detailed investigation into the Pakistani IP address to identify the person using it. Investigators initially examined the address as part of efforts to trace those involved in the suspicious online activity. However, they discovered that the person associated with the address was a victim rather than a perpetrator. The investigation subsequently led authorities to the 13-year-old girl, allowing them to intervene before she could carry out the instructions to harm herself. NCCIA officials said the girl's parents were completely unaware of her involvement with the online network until investigators contacted them. During questioning, the parents revealed that they had noticed changes in their daughter's behaviour over the previous six months but had not linked them to her online activities. The agency informed the family about the nature of the online interactions and the potential danger facing the teenager. NCCIA investigators are now working to trace the accounts used to contact the girl and establish the identities of those operating the suspected network. Officials said they were also examining whether other children in Pakistan had been targeted through similar online activities. The agency has not disclosed the identities or locations of the suspected operators, and no arrests have been announced as the investigation remains under way. The dark web is a hidden part of the internet that cannot be accessed through conventional search engines such as Google or Bing. It typically requires specialised software, such as the Tor browser, which helps users conceal their identities and online activities. While the dark web has legitimate uses, including private communication and bypassing censorship, it is also associated with illegal activities such as drug trafficking, weapons sales and cybercrime. Unlike the deep web, which includes private databases, emails and other content not indexed by search engines, the dark web is specifically designed to provide greater anonymity. Accessing the dark web is legal in most countries, but using it for criminal activities is not. Its anonymity can also expose users to online scams, malicious software and exploitation. title: In the bonfire of our emergencies
description: Published October 18, 2026 During a week that is rocked by the imposition of emergency and the governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, what event or revelation or thought has disturbed you the most? Have you lost sleep over something during this time? Or have you been too confused to decipher your own state of mind? Or do you just not care? If you take your cue from political pundits, the big event now is the (temporary?) removal of the PTI’s provincial government in KP through measures that lack democratic spirit. A detailed analysis of what this means would certainly be quite valid. There is this surge in terrorist violence in KP and also in Balochistan. Besides, the long march that was being led by the removed chief minister Sohail Afridi had also caused massive civic disruptions. But I am more concerned about cracks that are widening in our society, beyond politics. Here is something that could threaten the very survival of this country. In fact, I cannot understand why our rulers are not addressing these crises, which are getting more and more vicious. Do they not see that the Pakistani society is coming apart ats the seams? This has been my refrain, yes. But I will restrict myself to what has been reported in the media this week. I regret that I don’t have space to include all the headlines related to social decline and disorder. In recent years, we have fallen to the bottom of South Asia in many crucial social development indicators. The gap now appears to be widening. Does your heart not sink when you contemplate this reality? Perhaps the Peshawar tragedy in which at least 30 children and a female teacher were killed when the roof of a private school collapsed on Thursday does not belong in this tally. We may consider this an accident, though it also exemplifies the state of education in the country. We talk a lot about the constitution in the context of protecting democratic values, but what about the government’s constitutional responsibility to provide free primary education to all children in the country? Will there be a long march to demand this fundamental right? Anyhow, the Peshawar tragedy has deepened the gloom that is surrounding us. I do feel that this heartbreaking event also portrays a deprived and potentially flawed society. We see glimpses of growing poverty here, and this is my first reference to a headline I read in the print media on Tuesday. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) released the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) in New York on Monday. According to this index, 38.3% of Pakistan’s population was multidimensionally poor, compared with 16.4% in India and 14.9% in Bangladesh. I ask you to read these figures again, pause and think. The estimates are based on household surveys conducted in different years and do not provide a strictly contemporaneous comparison. What we gather, surely, is that more than one third of Pakistan’s population faces overlapping deprivations in health, education and living standards. The intensity of deprivation among those classified as multidimensionally poor stood at 51.7% in Pakistan. Another 12.5% of the population was considered vulnerable to multidimensional poverty, indicating that a substantial share of the people remained at risk of falling into acute deprivation. We have plenty of material in UNDP’s MPI report, but I’m moving on to another assessment from the World Economic Forum’s annual meeting of Global Future Leaders, which opened in Dubai on Tuesday. It includes a discussion on how to boost youth employment in Pakistan for the age of AI. It revealed that only 7% of Pakistan’s youth have access to formal technical and vocational training, compared with the regional average of 22%. Take another pause. We may also recall how our leaders have sometimes underlined the benefits of our pronounced youth bulge. The World Bank estimates that this skill gap costs Pakistan $31.5 billion annually in lost productivity and unrealised export potential. There is another report that can also be mentioned briefly. On Wednesday, the 2026 Global Hunger Index was released. This index is published jointly by a German institute and a Swiss organisation under the theme: “No security without food security”. In this report, Pakistan recorded the highest score in South Asia, reflecting a worsening food security crisis driven by economic instability, climate shocks, and global conflicts. Progress in South Asia has largely stagnated, with conditions in Pakistan and Afghanistan deteriorating since 2018. While child stunting remains very high in Pakistan and Afghanistan, it is noted that Pakistan’s stunting rate continues to fall whereas Afghanistan’s has edged up since 2018. This is hard to accept. Finally, I have a number of stories about violent crime and the kind of behaviour of that portrays mental health issues. In addition, it appears that cases of scams and fraud are increasing. Similarly, the crisis of child sex abuse and of rape of young women remains evident in reports from various parts of the country. But let me conclude with what was discovered in Karachi on Tuesday morning. Five members of a family were found dead inside their one-room house in a housing society that was locked from inside. The police said that a man and his wife had bullet wounds, while their little daughters, aged five and three, and the man’s younger sister bore no injury marks. There was a handwritten suicide note, with some blood on it, that mentioned severe financial difficulties. Incidentally, this seemed to be a replay of the mysterious deaths of a doctor, his wife and their three daughters in a locked apartment in another neighbourhood in Karachi last month. But these stories easily get lost in the noise our politicians and rulers make. The writer is a senior journalist. title: Billions for war, pennies for climate
description: Published October 16, 2026 Ghulam Sakina lives in a small straw-and-bamboo cottage on the coast of Sindh. There is no road traffic here, no nearby factory fumes, no crowds. However, she is among the people hit hardest by climate change. There is no clean drinking water, so she walks miles to get it. Her husband is a fisherman, but some days the nets come back empty. Hunger is visible on their tired faces. Far away, in a village in Gilgit-Baltistan, another woman lives beneath tall mountains. A flash flood washes away her home and nearly everything she owns. Most historical greenhouse gas emissions have come from industrialised countries, while China is now the world’s largest annual emitter. Yet the damage crosses borders and falls heavily on people like these two women. Pakistan produces less than 1% of global emissions, yet it pays a heavy price. The 2022 floods killed more than 1,700 people and affected 33 million. By early August 2026, at least 136 people had died in the monsoon-related incidents, according to the National Disaster Management Authority. So, the real test of climate diplomacy is simple: what changes in the lives of people like Sakina? From November 9 to 20, world leaders will meet for COP31 in Antalya, Turkiye. The COP process has delivered important agreements, most notably the Paris Agreement. But after more than three decades of climate negotiations, the gap between promises and implementation remains difficult to defend. Take the Loss and Damage Fund. At COP27 in 2022, countries agreed to it as a historic win for vulnerable nations. Four years later, pledges stand at about $822 million, and campaign groups say only about $449 million has been paid in as of April 2026. Experts say developing countries may need $200 to $400 billion every year to deal with climate losses. The pledges are a tiny fraction of that, and campaigners warn the fund could run dry by 2027. The story is similar elsewhere. At COP29, countries agreed to a new climate-finance goal of $300 billion a year for developing countries by 2035, while calling for efforts to scale total climate finance towards $1.3 trillion annually. At COP30 in Belem, countries agreed to push for a major increase in adaptation finance, but failed to agree on a clear roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels. Each year brings new commitments, while accountability for previous ones remains weak. Meanwhile, military budgets continue to expand. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) says the world spent a record $2.89 trillion on militaries in 2025, the eleventh increase in a row. That is nearly $8 billion every day. At that rate, the entire $822 million pledged to the Loss and Damage Fund represents less than three hours of global military spending. Now look at this year. The US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, 2026. The US Congressional Budget Office says it cost the Pentagon more than $38 billion by August 1, and it still adds about $3 billion a month. That is roughly forty-six times everything pledged to the Loss and Damage Fund, and it counts only one side’s costs. War also hurts the climate directly. Bombs, burning oil facilities and fighter jets release huge amounts of carbon. One research group estimated that the first two weeks of the Iran war alone produced more than five million tonnes of carbon dioxide, more than Iceland emits in a year. Military emissions are also largely missing from the reports that countries send to the UN. Rebuilding demolished cities adds still more pollution later. Then there is the cost to ordinary people. Wars push up fuel and food prices, and energy-importing countries like Pakistan feel it quickly. When budgets are stretched, climate promises are usually the first to be cut. Military spending and climate finance are not interchangeable budget lines, and governments have legitimate security responsibilities. The comparison is nevertheless revealing. It shows what the international system can mobilise when leaders perceive a threat as an immediate security priority. Climate vulnerability deserves similar urgency, particularly in countries where floods, droughts, heatwaves and water insecurity already threaten lives and livelihoods. War and climate change, then, are not separate problems. War drains the money that could protect people and adds to the pollution that endangers them. That is why I suggest that COP31 should put the climate-security nexus higher on the agenda as a major theme. This does not need to be only a slogan. The first step is honest counting: countries should report military emissions openly, like any other source of pollution. The second is moving a small share of money. If just 1% of global military spending went to climate-affected communities, it would come to about $29 billion a year, which is thirty-five times what the Loss and Damage Fund has been promised up to now. The talks also need honest tracking. A public yearly report should show what each country promised, what it paid, and what actually reached communities. Finally, money must reach the people who need it. It should flow directly to local, community-led solutions such as clean water and flood-resistant homes, climate-smart agriculture, instead of getting stuck in reports and consultants’ fees. Climate diplomacy matters, and the people working through these negotiations deserve credit for the agreements already achieved. But the climate crisis is moving faster than the pace of implementation. COP must now match the scale and urgency of the emergency it was created to address. Ghulam Sakina will not follow the negotiations in Antalya. She will wake up tomorrow, walk miles for water and hope the fish come back. If COP31 cannot reach people like her, then climate diplomacy has not yet reached its purpose. It is time to recognise that the security of people like Sakina is also security, and that climate resilience deserves the political urgency and resources the world can mobilise for other threats. title: Strong earthquake hits China's Tibet, killing 16 people
description:
Published October 23, 2026     A magnitude 7 earthquake struck China's Tibet region on Thursday night, killing at least 16 people and injuring 32 others, state news agency Xinhua reported, citing Nagqu City's emergency management bureau. As of 2:25 am on Friday, 11 of the injured were in serious condition, while 21 sustained minor injuries, Xinhua reported. Local authorities found at least two people injured in a village near the epicentre, with some houses in villages closest to the epicentre showing cracks, the state broadcaster said. The quake was the strongest to hit China since January 2024. The epicentre was in a sparsely populated, high-altitude county in Nagqu, northern Tibet, at a depth of 10 km (6.2 miles). The average elevation within 5 km of the epicentre is about 4,864 metres (15,960 feet), data from the China Earthquake Networks Centre (CENC) showed. Videos released by local state-run media showed people leaving their homes and seeking shelter outside or in cars parked on the street. One resident reported being awakened by the strong quake and hearing the house creaking during the tremor. The quake was clearly felt in the local area, CENC said. The epicentre was around 400 km from the Tibetan capital, Lhasa. Local fire and rescue teams have been mobilised and are heading to the affected region, state media said. A series of smaller tremors of around magnitude 3 and 4 were recorded in surrounding regions following the magnitude 7 earthquake, CENC data showed. title: Canada, Turkiye sign 'strategic partnership' as part of Carney push to cut reliance on US
description:
Published October 22, 2026 Nato allies Canada and Turkiye upgraded their relations to a "strategic partnership" during the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister on Thursday, as Mark Carney seeks new global trade partners to reduce reliance on the United States. The new partnership signed in Ankara focuses on trade and investment, defence and security, energy, and social and diplomatic ties. It aims to create jobs and opportunities for Canadian and Turkish companies to do more business together. Carney is on a global trade blitz that he hopes will help buffer Canada from a trade war with the US, where President Donald Trump has applied sweeping tariffs and questioned the neighbouring country's sovereignty. Speaking next to Erdogan at Turkiye's presidential palace, Carney said the strategic partnership would have four pillars and include a three-year action plan. "We've planted the seeds of something new: a strategic partnership that will create new opportunities for our workers and businesses, and greater security and prosperity for both our peoples. With care and commitment, it will grow for generations to come," Carney said. At the ceremony, Canadian and Turkish ministers signed cooperation deals on energy, defence and air transport. The agreement by Carney and Turkiye President Tayyip Erdogan marks a significant thaw in diplomatic ties that had long been cool over Canadian concerns over human rights and a past embargo on sending weapons to Turkiye. Turkiye, a major emerging market economy and regional military power, is seeking new investment and collaboration for its burgeoning defence industry, new nuclear power plants and mining sector. Erdogan, who has led Turkiye for 23 years, praised Carney as a leader with "common-sense and acumen" on the world political stage. "Today, we have alleviated the long-standing Turkiye-Canada disconnect. Now, we are starting a new era between Turkiye and Canada," Erdogan said. The two sides expected to raise their trade volume from $3 billion first to $5 billion and then to $10 billion, he said, without giving a timeframe. Canadian and Turkish negotiators will kick off the first round of free trade talks next month in Ankara, Carney said, adding that Export Development Canada and Turkiye's Eximbank would sign a new deal to boost companies' cooperation on projects in third nations. Carney referenced the need to move forward with Turkiye amid the "rupture" and "new world order", though neither he nor Erdogan mentioned the United States. Carney will meet prominent Turkish business leaders and investors in Istanbul on Friday. In the energy sector, Canada and Turkiye pledged to ramp up collaboration in areas such as nuclear energy, critical minerals, and liquefied natural gas (LNG). Reuters first reported this week that the countries planned to sign a declaration deepening cooperation in the four areas outlined on Thursday. Although trade between Canada and Turkiye is tiny — Turkiye accounted for less than 0.3% of Canada's total merchandise trade or C$4.34 billion ($3.09 billion) – bilateral trade has risen by nearly 50% in the past five years. Still, Canada sends nearly 70% of exports to the US. "This trip is part of the geopolitical necessity of signalling to Americans that we are not sitting around waiting for them," said Bessma Momani, professor of political science at the University of Waterloo. In the last year, Canada has signed more than 20 trade deals as part of Carney's push to double non-US exports in the next decade. At the Nato leaders' summit in July, Carney and Erdogan launched negotiations for a free-trade agreement and Turkiye also agreed to join Canada's Defence, Security and Resilience Bank as a founding member. Turkiye has held talks with Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRealis as well as South Korea's Korea Electric Power Corporation and China's State Power Investment Corporation about potentially building its planned second and third nuclear power plants. In 2024, Canada removed weapons-export controls on Turkiye, including on optical technology used in drones that Turkiye exports to dozens of nations. Canada mainly exports lentils, aircraft and electronics to Turkiye, and imports medical devices, fishing vessels, aircraft engines and jewellery. Copyright © 2026. Geo Television Network. title: IMF sees 1.3% contraction in Pakistan, Middle East and North Africa in 2026
description:
Published October 22, 2026 DUBAI: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Thursday forecast a sharp drop in economic output in the Middle East, North Africa and Pakistan this year due to the US-Israeli-led war against Iran, followed by a rebound to 6.6% growth in 2027, while warning that further energy production disruptions could worsen the outlook. The IMF said the region's output was expected to contract by 1.3% as a result of the war's impact on energy production, shipping, tourism, trade and confidence. Economic output would increase sharply in 2027, but output in those economies would generally stay below pre-war projections. The war's impact had been substantial, but uneven, with oil-exporting economies directly affected by disruptions to energy production and shipping hit harder, and oil importers proving to be more resilient, the IMF said in its regional outlook released on Thursday in Dubai. The IMF said its baseline assumed that the conflict would abate in early 2027 and that trade would gradually normalise during the year, but it said the outlook remained clouded by "exceptionally high uncertainty." "The main risks derive from further disruption to energy production and trade routes that could drive energy prices higher," the IMF said in a statement outlining its key messages, noting external financial conditions could also tighten. External financial conditions could also tighten if investors reassess AI-driven productivity gains and interest rates rise further amid heightened concerns about inflation and fiscal positions, it said. Oil importers had proven more resilient, with domestic demand supported by remittances and tourism flows, favourable financial conditions, and prompt policy responses that safeguard consumers from higher commodity prices, the IMF said. Growth in the Caucasus and Central Asia was moderating towards a more sustainable pace, the IMF said, forecasting a 5.2% rise in economic output in 2026 and 5% in 2027. The IMF underscored the mantra it delivered during last week's annual meetings, urging policymakers to prioritise maintaining price stability, while preserving fiscal sustainability, maintaining central bank independence and enacting structural reforms to boost productivity and create jobs. title: LPG cylinders selling at over twice official price amid supply crisis: sources
description:
Published October 21, 2026 ISLAMABAD: Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) cylinders are being sold at more than twice the official price across the country as disrupted imports trigger a supply crisis, sources in the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) told Geo News on Wednesday. Ogra has fixed the price of an 11.8kg domestic LPG cylinder at Rs3,296, while sources said cylinders were currently being sold at more than double that rate. According to Ogra sources, the crisis emerged following the closure of the Iranian border, disrupting supplies from a country that accounts for 50% of Pakistan’s total LPG imports. Pakistan imports around 70% of its LPG requirements, with supplies coming from Iran, Iraq and Oman, the sources said. They warned that the crisis could worsen if the Iranian border was not reopened for LPG imports. Meanwhile, LPG imports from Oman and Iraq had also been disrupted due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the sources added. Ogra sources attributed the surge in LPG prices to the supply disruption, saying enforcement teams were taking action against those overcharging for available stocks. Pakistan’s average annual LPG consumption stands at between 2.4 million and 2.5 million tonnes, according to the sources. Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik, meanwhile, said the world was going through “extraordinary circumstances” concerning energy prices and that government measures on LPG prices would become visible soon. Appearing on Geo News’ programme “Capital Talk”, he said Pakistan consumed around 6,500 to 7,000 tonnes of LPG daily, of which around 2,000 to 2,500 tonnes were produced locally and the remainder imported. Malik said LPG should be priced between Rs400 and Rs425 per kilogramme and vowed action against those charging excessive rates. “Those overcharging for LPG will face action,” he said, adding that the government was fully prepared to deal with profiteers. The minister said the government would itself import LPG and bring it into the system, predicting that an improvement in prices would begin within two to three days. He said the government would also bring transparency to LPG pricing similar to that of petrol. Malik claimed the difference between market and local LPG prices amounted to Rs30 billion, accusing a small number of people of exploiting consumers after obtaining stay orders. “A few people are sitting like vultures after obtaining stay orders and sucking the public’s blood,” the minister said. He said the government had warned them until September and again urged them to provide LPG at a fair price. According to Malik, the prime minister had tasked the attorney general with pursuing the remaining cases to have the stay orders vacated. The petroleum minister also said Pakistan previously received 1,000mmcfd of gas from Qatar, while pointing to the prevailing situation in the Strait of Hormuz. Despite the difficulties, he said, Qatar had supplied gas to Pakistan at $12 to $13 instead of $30. Malik said the government had devised a strategy for gas supplies from November to February, with efforts aimed at ensuring consumers continued receiving gas during all three meal preparation periods. He added that funds had been allocated for the fuel subsidy and that considerable room remained within the budget. Copyright © 2026. Geo Television Network. All Rights Reserved.

title: Maradona doctor was made 'scapegoat' for his death, Argentine court told
description:
Published October 22, 2026 SAN ISIDRO, ARGENTINA: A lawyer for Leopoldo Luque, a doctor charged in the 2020 death of Argentine football legend Diego Maradona, said in closing arguments on Wednesday that his client was innocent and had been made a "scapegoat." Attorney Roberto Rallin rejected the prosecution's argument that Maradona's November 2020 death was foreseeable, while another defence attorney, Francisco Oneto, maintained that his death resulted from an "acute and unpredictable" heart attack. "There was absolutely no possibility of predicting this fatal outcome," Oneto insisted. Prosecutors have requested a 12-year prison sentence for Luque, a neurosurgeon considered a key decision-maker for Maradona at the time of his death. "We are here to proclaim Luque's innocence, not with television slogans, but with the evidence that supports it," Rallin said. "Leopoldo Luque has been the scapegoat." Maradona died at age 60 from a cardiorespiratory crisis coupled with pulmonary edema. He was found dead in his bed at a residence in Tigre, north of Buenos Aires, rented for his convalescence, following surgery for a subdural hematoma. The death of Argentina's favourite son plunged the country into mourning in the midst of the Covid-19 pandemic. Tens of thousands of people defied social distancing rules to bid farewell to him as he lay in state at the presidential palace. A total of seven health-care professionals have been on trial since April for potential negligence leading to the star's death during his two weeks of convalescence. Prosecutors have requested sentences ranging from four to 12 years for six of the seven defendants. In its closing arguments, the prosecution condemned Luque's "inaction," saying his attitude "was always to do nothing" in the face of the warning signs that Maradona was exhibiting. Luque's lawyers particularly attacked the conclusions of the interdisciplinary medical commission, which had been established by the court in 2021 to provide an opinion on the star's death. The commission, which based its findings on the autopsy and other things, said Maradona had a history of heart problems that should have been taken into account, a conclusion the prosecution emphasised. But Luque's defence lawyers said that clinical tests done prior to Maradona's surgery just before his death didn't reveal any heart issues. "It's so clear that Maradona didn't have any heart problems in 2020," Oneto said during closing arguments. Throughout the trial, Luque was by far the most combative defendant, speaking several times when he felt he was being implicated. His legal team played audio recordings, presented scientific articles and even a video of Maradona's autopsy, provoking the anger of the footballer's daughters. "It's easy to attack me because I'm the one who had the most contact with Maradona," Luque said in court, asserting that "the only one who would defend me would be Diego." "I cared deeply for him, I loved him, he was my idol and my friend," he said. Defence attorney Nicolas D'Albora, who represents medical coordinator Nancy Forlini, also blamed Maradona's demise on Luque and another doctor, saying they "were obliged to guarantee the patient's health." Forlini faces a 10-year sentence for homicide with eventual intent, for an alleged failure to provide basic medical equipment for home care. The defence's closing arguments are expected to continue until Thursday. Copyright © 2026. Geo Television Network. All Rights Reserved.

title: The art of economic statecraft
description: Published October 19, 2026 Every generation in its time inherits a different economic question. The 19th century is defined by industrialisation; the 20th is marked by production, trade and globalisation. The 21st century brought us a new paradigm: not how nations create wealth, but how they preserve, multiply and protect their wealth, in times of geopolitical rivalry, technological disruption and climate risk. Economic statecraft focuses on the disciplined coordination of public institutions, national capital and strategic policy to create, protect and maximise national wealth across generations. It differs from economic management because it prepares nations for tomorrow’s opportunities and risks, while economic management primarily addresses today’s problems. Under economic statecraft, fiscal policy, financial markets, industrial strategy, technology and national security are not considered as separate disciplines but interconnected instruments of national power. Nations do not prosper because they have abundant natural resources, nor do they disappear because they run out of wealth; all depends upon the quality of institutions that govern their economic management. From a historical perspective, modern public finance was pioneered by the Dutch Republic; credible fiscal institutions and deep capital markets laid the foundations of Britain’s Industrial Revolution; through sophisticated financial markets, the US transformed private enterprise into global economic leadership. In recent times, countries with different histories and resource endowments – Singapore, South Korea, Norway and the UAE – can achieve extraordinary success through disciplined institutions, efficient capital allocation and long-term policy continuity. Sustainable prosperity is eventually an institutional accomplishment. The parameters of the global economy are being reshaped once again. Trade, technology and investment between the US and China are redefining the strategic competition. This is reshaping supply chains worldwide, which are increasingly organised around resilience as much as efficiency. Artificial intelligence is another important factor transforming productivity; digital finance is constantly reshaping financial systems; and investment decisions and sovereign borrowing are influenced by climate considerations. Sovereign investment has also become an instrument of foreign policy, with states increasingly positioning sovereign wealth funds, development finance institutions and export credit agencies to secure technology, energy security, critical minerals and strategic partnerships. Economic strength today rests on two important factors: growth and institutional capability. Pakistan has the advantage of a strategic geopolitical location. It sits at the crossroads of South Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East and China; Pakistan has strategic geography, entrepreneurial talent, abundant resources, and a youthful population. These changes present both a challenge and an opportunity for us; however, they will create opportunity only if institutions can convert national potential into lasting economic strength. Modern economic statecraft rests on seven mutually reinforcing pillars: the first is the nation’s sovereign finance. The national balance sheet must include national assets and liabilities, not just annual budgets and public debt. Norway transformed petroleum revenues and wealth into one of the world’s largest sovereign wealth funds, while Singapore, through GIC, and the UAE, through ADIA, show how professional management of public assets can build long-term national wealth. Pakistan also possesses valuable public assets, from land and infrastructure to mineral resources and state-owned enterprises, but unfortunately, they remain underutilised because fragmented institutional arrangements manage them. For instance, circular debt, the protracted restructuring of Pakistan Steel Mills and the cyclical losses of PIA demonstrate the cost of managing public liabilities without adequate plans and policies for public assets. The second pillar is macroeconomic policy objectives. Sustainable growth requires fiscal, monetary, trade, industrial and labour-market policies to strengthen and harmonise one another rather than function independently. Successful economies achieve durable prosperity not only through reforms but through consistent policy, which in turn encourages investment, innovation and productivity. Pakistan’s economy has struggled with a lack of continuity and consistency in policy for quite some time. The third pillar is capital-market development. Modern economies rely not only on banks but also on corporate bond markets, pension funds, insurance companies, venture capital, infrastructure funds and Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) to transform domestic savings into productive investment. Mature capital markets finance entrepreneurship, innovation and productivity while lessening excessive dependence on commercial banking. The fourth pillar is macroprudential regulation. The global financial crisis revealed that financial stability cannot be fortified simply by overseeing individual institutions. Systemic risks emerge across interconnected markets through leverage, liquidity pressures and external shocks. Effective macroprudential governance therefore demands continuous coordination between the Ministry of Finance, the State Bank of Pakistan, the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan and other regulators to anticipate risks before they become crises. The fifth pillar is industrial strategy, as competitive economies foster structural transformation and carefully develop comparative advantage by positioning investment, research, innovation, export finance, infrastructure and skilled human capital with sectors capable of engendering persistent productivity growth. For Pakistan’s prospective, agriculture value addition, minerals, advanced manufacturing, logistics, digital services and export-oriented industries should become central pillars of long-term sustainable development. The sixth pillar is technological competitiveness. Artificial intelligence, digital payments, cybersecurity and financial technology are becoming significant catalysts of productivity, competitiveness and national resilience. AI will not beat the human race; rather, those who know how to use it will beat those who do not. Countries that invest early in digital capabilities will shape the future economy rather than be driven by events and merely adapt to it. The seventh and most important pillar is institutional governance. Strong institutions do not operate in isolation. Ministries of finance, FBR, State Bank, regulators, planning authorities, revenue agencies and investment institutions must function within a shared strategic framework. Integrated, professional coordination among these bodies distinguishes resilient economies from vulnerable ones. Pakistan’s repeated economic challenges – fiscal deficits, balance-of-payments pressures, underperforming SOEs, low FDI, shallow capital markets and fragmented policymaking, etc. – should therefore be understood not as isolated failures but as symptoms of an institutional deficit. The challenge is not to create completely new institutions and bodies, but to modernise, integrate, connect and align those that already exist.
