title: A home to build on
description:
Published October 17, 2026 When we speak about poverty, we often focus on income. Yet poverty is also about insecurity, exclusion and vulnerability. It is the absence of the conditions that allow people to live with dignity, access opportunities and build a better future for their families. This year’s International Day for the Eradication of Poverty, observed under the theme ‘Safe Homes for All’, highlights a fundamental but often overlooked truth: adequate housing is not only a human right, but it is also a foundation for inclusive development. A safe home provides far more than shelter. It creates the stability that lets children attend school, families access healthcare, communities participate in economic life and people withstand shocks that can push them deeper into poverty. Without safe and secure housing, many other development gains become difficult to sustain. In Sindh, the connection between housing, vulnerability and poverty became painfully clear during the devastating floods of 2022. The province accounted for 88% of the 2.1 million houses destroyed nationwide. Nearly half of Sindh’s 44,000 government schools were affected, more than 500 health facilities were damaged or destroyed, and millions of people saw their livelihoods disrupted. This understanding is reflected in the European Union-funded Poverty Alleviation and Inclusive Development Across Rural Sindh (PAIDAR) programme, implemented by the United Nations Industrial Development Organization has partnered with the Sindh People’s Housing for Flood Affectees (SPHF) programme to support recovery in flood-affected communities. While the SPHF is reconstructing climate-resilient homes for thousands of families, PAIDAR is helping ensure that these homes are embedded within safe, resilient and thriving settlements. Through Climate Resilient Settlement Development Plans (CRSDPs), housing reconstruction is complemented by investments in infrastructure, public services and livelihood opportunities, recognising that a truly safe home extends beyond four walls and a roof. Importantly, CRSDPs reflect all three priorities highlighted in this year’s global call to action. First, the observance calls on governments and development partners to make safe housing a human-rights priority. For vulnerable communities, the difference between secure and inadequate housing can determine whether climate shocks become temporary setbacks or long-term drivers of poverty. CRSDPs seek to reduce that vulnerability by supporting safer, more resilient living environments that protect lives, assets and livelihoods. Second, the observance calls for designing policies with people experiencing poverty. This principle is at the core of the CRSDP process. Village residents are not passive beneficiaries; they actively participate in identifying priorities, shaping investments, and overseeing implementation. The plans are developed through extensive community consultations, with women playing a central role in decision-making. Third, the observance calls for greater efforts to mobilise resources for safe homes for all. PAIDAR demonstrates how partnerships can translate this ambition into action. Through the programme, UNIDO has invested five million euros in communal infrastructure across flood-affected settlements, complementing seven million euros in climate-resilient housing reconstruction delivered through SPHF. The impact of this approach is already visible in Lakho Bhambhro, a village in Thatta district inaugurated earlier this year as Sindh’s first climate-resilient settlement. In many ways, the settlement brings to life the ambitions behind this year’s International Day for the Eradication of Poverty and its call for safe homes, community participation and greater investment in resilient communities. The significance of this work extends beyond Sindh. In 2025, world leaders adopted the Doha Political Declaration at the Second World Summit for Social Development, reaffirming the right to an adequate standard of living, including safe, accessible and affordable housing, water, sanitation and other essential services. During the summit, PAIDAR’s Climate Resilient Settlement Development Planning approach was showcased to global audiences as an example of how integrated, community-led development can help translate these commitments into action on the ground. Today, detailed CRSDPs have been prepared for 215 villages across Sindh, covering nearly 17,000 households, while implementation is advancing in 75 villages across Badin, Sujawal, Thatta, Larkana and Tharparkar. These investments represent more than physical infrastructure. They are investments in dignity, resilience, social inclusion and long-term prosperity. As we mark this year’s International Day for the Eradication of Poverty, the message is clear: ending poverty requires more than addressing immediate needs. It requires creating the conditions that enable people and communities to withstand shocks, seize opportunities and build secure futures. For rural communities across Sindh, that vision is already taking shape through CRSDPs. The challenge now is to scale it, sustain it and ensure that no one is left behind. The author is the national technical adviser at the United Nations Industrial Development Organisation (UNIDO). title: World Bank warns Middle East conflict could strain Pakistan's economy
description:
Published October 22, 2026 ISLAMABAD: A prolonged conflict in the Middle East could intensify economic pressures on Pakistan by keeping global energy prices high, increasing import costs and putting further strain on the country’s external financing and foreign exchange reserves, the World Bank has warned. In its report, "Pakistan Development Update: Attaining Escape Velocity", the World Bank identified a longer or more intense conflict as the biggest risk to Pakistan’s near-term macroeconomic outlook. The conflict — which began on February 28, 2026, when the United States and Israel launched coordinated strikes against Iran — has heightened risks to global energy supplies and prices, with Pakistan particularly exposed because of its reliance on imported petroleum and gas. Tehran responded with retaliatory attacks against Israel and the US assets in the region as tensions escalated across the Middle East. The hostilities disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global oil and gas supplies, raising concerns over energy security and driving up international prices. According to the World Bank’s report, Pakistan’s petroleum and gas products accounted for around one-quarter of the country’s total imports in fiscal year 2025, equivalent to 3.7% of gross domestic product (GDP), while Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries supplied around 80% of these imports. The report said that Pakistan’s petroleum import group increased by 9.2% year-on-year during January–June 2026, while the import bill for crude petroleum surged by 46.4% over the same period, the report said. The economic impact has been reflected in Pakistan’s import bill. By the end of June 2026, oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) prices had risen significantly compared with pre-conflict levels. The World Bank warned that a longer or more intense conflict could sustain elevated energy prices, widen the current account deficit and put additional pressure on foreign exchange reserves. Disruptions to trade routes and weaker export demand could further weigh on economic activity, while higher input costs could fuel inflation and erode household purchasing power. Separately, the World Bank warned that a stronger-than-expected El Nino could threaten Pakistan’s agricultural output and economic growth. El Nino is a climate phenomenon involving the periodic warming of sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, which can alter weather patterns worldwide and increase the risk of droughts, heatwaves or excessive rainfall in different regions. The World Bank's baseline projection puts real GDP growth at 3.8% in FY2027. Under the crop-output scenario described in the report, zero growth in crop output could reduce growth by 0.2 percentage points to 3.6%. This is a conditional scenario, not the baseline forecast. The report added that Pakistan’s existing external buffers could help absorb additional import requirements arising from an agricultural shock, although doing so could significantly deplete foreign exchange reserves. title: Sri Lanka pull off second-highest chase in ODI history against England
description:
Published October 22, 2026 Sri Lanka produced a sensational batting performance to chase down England’s mammoth target of 430 runs in the third ODI of the tri-nation series at Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Thursday, completing a remarkable victory with one ball to spare. Sri Lanka reached the target in 49.5 overs, pulling off what was billed as the second-highest successful run chase in ODI history after England had posted an imposing 429 for four in their allotted 50 overs. Sri Lanka endured a shaky start to their pursuit, losing opener Kamindu Mendis for 18 and skipper Kusal Mendis for a duck within the first five overs, leaving the team struggling at 24 runs. However, Rathnayake joined Fernando at the crease, and the pair launched a spirited counterattack against the England bowlers. Their third-wicket stand yielded 166 runs from just 137 deliveries, with both batters reaching their respective half-centuries. The partnership was finally broken by Jamie Overton on the opening delivery of the 28th over, when he caught Fernando off his own bowling. Fernando departed after a brilliant 83-ball knock of 97, featuring 11 boundaries and two sixes. Dasun Shanaka arrived at number five following Fernando's dismissal and combined with Rathnayake to maintain Sri Lanka's scoring momentum. The pair added a rapid 133 runs for the fourth wicket, during which Rathnayake advanced from his half-century to register his second ODI hundred. Sam Curran eventually ended Rathnayake's outstanding innings in the 41st over. The opener finished as Sri Lanka's leading scorer with 130 off 106 balls, striking 15 fours and three sixes. Shanaka continued his aggressive approach in partnership with Janith Liyanage, adding another 40 runs for the fifth wicket. However, the all-rounder narrowly missed out on his maiden ODI century, falling for 97 to Liam Dawson. His explosive 50-ball innings included six fours and eight sixes. After Shanaka's departure, Liyanage took charge of the chase and guided Sri Lanka across the finish line. He remained unbeaten on 61 from just 27 deliveries, hitting seven fours and three sixes, as the visitors sealed victory on the penultimate ball of the innings. For England, Josh Tongue led the bowling effort with figures of three wickets for 79 runs in 8.5 overs. Curran claimed two wickets, while Overton and Dawson picked up one wicket each. Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis's decision to field first backfired as the Three Lions racked up 429/4 in their 50 overs, which was then the highest total in the host country, surpassing the previous best of 375/3, which the host nation Pakistan recorded against Zimbabwe in 2015. England got off to a blazing start to their innings as their opening pair of Tom Banton and Ben Duckett shared a brisk 74-run partnership before both fell victim to Dunith Wellalage in the spinner's successive overs. Banton, who dominated the opening stand, walked back after scoring a 50-ball 51 with the help of nine fours, while Duckett contributed with 29 off 39 deliveries. Following the back-to-back dismissals, captain Brook and experienced Joe Root took the reins of England's batting charge, and the duo put the 2019 champions in complete control by raising a 159-run partnership for the third wicket, during which both batters brought up their respective half-centuries. Asitha Fernando eventually broke the threatening partnership on the first delivery of the 38th over by dismissing Root, who departed after scoring 69 off 66 deliveries, smashing eight boundaries. Skipper Brook, meanwhile, stood his ground firmly and decimated Sri Lanka's bowling attack in the concluding phase of the innings, alongside all-rounder Will Jacks, ensuring England breached the 400-run barrier, as they shared an 185-run partnership off 77 deliveries, which concluded on the final delivery of the innings with the former's dismissal off Janith Liyanage. title: Pakistan receives second Qatar LNG cargo in October, aims to avoid costly spot purchases
description:
Published October 22, 2026     Pakistan has received its second liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargo from Qatar this month, with gas supplies from the shipment already being injected into the national system, Ministry of Energy sources said on Thursday. The arrival comes as the government seeks to maintain gas supplies while avoiding expensive purchases from the international spot market, where LNG prices can reach $30 per million British thermal units (MMBtu), the sources said. LNG imported under Pakistan’s existing agreement with Qatar costs around $14 to $15 per MMBtu, roughly half the reported spot-market price, they added. The ministry sources said the government was making every effort to avoid buying LNG at higher spot-market rates and was relying on contracted Qatari supplies to meet the country’s energy requirements. Pakistan received its first LNG cargo of October on October 14, when the vessel Al-Areesh berthed at Engro’s LNG terminal and regasification began, restoring supplies of around 150 million cubic feet per day to the national gas network, according to earlier reports. The second October shipment follows continued uncertainty over LNG imports amid disruptions to regional energy supplies and shipping routes. QatarEnergy declared force majeure in March following damage to its Ras Laffan facility during the regional conflict, affecting contracted supplies to several customers, including Pakistan. The interruptions have raised concerns about Pakistan’s ability to meet rising gas demand during the coming winter. The country relies on imported LNG to supplement domestic gas production and supply fuel to power plants and other consumers. Pakistan has been exploring additional cargoes to strengthen supplies, but higher international prices could increase the cost of imports if contracted shipments remain insufficient. The latest cargo provides some relief, although the overall supply outlook remains dependent on the availability of further shipments and the country’s ability to secure LNG at affordable rates. title: Bones from Iraqi cave hint at violence and compassion in Neanderthals
description:
Published October 15, 2026 The bones of a Neanderthal from a cave in Iraq's Kurdistan region offer evidence of both violence and compassion in the closest evolutionary cousins of our species, exhibiting a wound apparently from a fatal spear attack as well as signs of an earlier nonfatal injury that may have elicited kindly care. Researchers have discovered at Shanidar Cave in the Zagros Mountains of northern Iraq a partial skeleton of a Neanderthal, aged in the mid-40s, that included a left shoulder blade, or scapula, with a circular hole six-tenths of an inch (15 mm) wide indicative of a deeply penetrating stab. The bones of this individual, who they call Shanidar A, were unearthed from under about 25 feet (7.5 meters) of rocks and sediment inside the cave and date to about 75,000 years ago. The researchers were unable to determine Shanidar A's sex. The researchers said the injury's shape suggests it was caused by a forceful thrust using a sharpened wooden spear, a type of weapon Neanderthals are known to have used, rather than a spear with a stone tip. It was a weapon employed in hunting large mammals that were an important food source. "The spear would have gone through the skin and major muscles, especially the pectoralis, as well as the ribcage and muscles between the ribs, and the lung," said biological anthropologist Emma Pomeroy of the University of Cambridge in England, lead author of the study published on Thursday in the journal Scientific Reports . "The location could be like the kind of 'heart shot' hunters use to kill animals quickly by puncturing the heart, but that is a bit speculative. We do see heart shots as a hunting strategy both today and in the archaeological record. Neanderthals would have known this would lead to a quick death," Pomeroy said. University of Cambridge archaeologist and study co-author Graeme Barker, who has led Shanidar Cave excavations since 2015, said the likeliest scenario is interpersonal violence. The researchers said the violence probably occurred either between members of a particular Neanderthal group or between members of rival Neanderthal groups, calling a Homo sapiens attack or an accidental injury less likely. The researchers found shards of bone displaced by the weapon. The injury indicated that the spear entered from above with a downward trajectory, penetrating the left chest cavity from the front and traveling through the body before punching the hole in the scapula, causing quick death. In addition to the scapula, the researchers found some ribs, a nearly complete right hand and seven teeth, mostly from the front of the lower jaw, belonging to Shanidar A. The teeth bore evidence that this Neanderthal had survived brutal injury at least a year before death — a blow to the face resulting in front teeth being smashed and lost. One tooth was split, with half remaining rotated in the mouth and others pushed out of position. "The pain would have been extreme, and basic needs like eating and drinking would have been difficult, perhaps meaning Shanidar A needed food mashing and being able to rest. It's likely that Shanidar A did need some care from members of the group for some basic needs during recovery," Pomeroy said. Shanidar A was one of five Neanderthals, four adults and one infant, whose bodies were carefully tucked behind a rock pillar in the cave in a burial cluster within a generation or so of each other. The cave was occupied by Neanderthals for tens of thousands of years as a seasonal campsite, and later by Homo sapiens. Neanderthals were more robustly built than Homo sapiens, with larger brows. They lived as hunter-gatherers and inhabited Eurasia from the Atlantic coast to the Ural Mountains from about 400,000 years ago until a bit after 40,000 years ago, disappearing after Homo sapiens became established in the region. The two species interbred, with modern non-African human populations bearing residual Neanderthal DNA. The cave, overlooking the Great Zab river valley, has been a source of information about Neanderthals since the 1950s, with Shanidar A now offering new insight into their behavior. "We see evidence of two contrasting facets of human nature — care and violence — juxtaposed in the same individual," Pomeroy said. "We see evidence all around us today that violence and care are both aspects of how we humans behave, and we see this here in Shanidar A, too. Neanderthals were like us in many respects, both the good and the bad, and this find really highlights that, going against stereotypes of Neanderthals as unintelligent, uncaring cavemen and cavewomen," Pomeroy said. title: Isle of Wight fossil sheds light on enigmatic meat-eating dinosaurs
description:
Published October 14, 2026 The partial skull of a tiger-sized predator that prowled what is now the Isle of Wight off England's southern coast about 120 million years ago is giving scientists a better understanding of an enigmatic group of meat-eating dinosaurs known for running down prey and ripping them apart with massive hand claws. Researchers said the fossil belongs to a species they have ‌named Invictibellatrix amberina, an early member of the lineage of Cretaceous Period carnivorous dinosaurs called megaraptorans. Invictibellatrix adds to the knowledge of skull anatomy among early megaraptorans and, being the first one known from Europe, helps show how the group spread globally. Invictibellatrix is one of the smallest megaraptorans. Based on fossils of closely related megaraptorans, the researchers estimated that Invictibellatrix was about 16 feet (5 meters) long, with the weight of a large tiger. Its body may have been covered in filament-like feathers, they said. Megaraptorans were part of the group called theropods that spans all the meat-eating dinosaurs. "Megaraptorans are very unique among theropods because they have relatively small and slender heads but had long and strong arms with massive hand claws as well as very lightly built ⁠skeletons," said Cassius Morrison, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Leeds in England and lead author of the study published in the journal Royal Society Open Science. "These characteristics imply that megaraptorans were agile hunters capable of chasing down prey and using their large arms and claws to catch them and disembowel them using their hand claws," Morrison said. The largest-known megaraptoran, named Maip, was about 33 feet (10 meters) long, inhabiting Patagonia during the twilight of the dinosaur age, about 50 million years after Invictibellatrix lived. Littler megaraptorans like Invictibellatrix may have hunted smaller prey like mammals, smaller reptiles and baby dinosaurs. Larger megaraptorans may have targeted bigger plant-eating dinosaurs like duckbilled hadrosaurs and long-necked sauropods, though probably not the biggest ones. Megaraptorans hunted in the opposite way from massive predators like Tyrannosaurus rex. Tyrannosaurus employed its large and stoutly built head, enormous teeth and incredible bite strength to kill prey, but had puny arms of little use in hunting. Invictibellatrix was not the Isle of Wight's top predator, with larger theropods around, alongside various herbivorous dinosaurs, and may have filled a role similar to a hyena today. There is a debate among dinosaur palaeontologists as to where megaraptorans fit on the theropod family tree. Despite differences in how ‌they were built ⁠and hunted, one hypothesis is that megaraptorans were closely related to tyrannosaurs, the group that included Tyrannosaurus and others that dominated the landscapes in North America and Asia later in the Cretaceous. Invictibellatrix means "unconquered female warrior." Morrison noted that after humble beginnings, megaraptorans developed into apex predators in South America, Australia and Antarctica, becoming "the ruling queens," while the tyrannosaurs became the "tyrant kings" in North America and Asia. Scientists are trying to unravel the evolutionary history of megaraptorans. A leading hypothesis has megaraptorans originating in Asia before migrating through Europe into Africa and then on into South America, thriving until the dinosaurs were doomed by an asteroid strike 66 million years ago. ⁠This hypothesis was lacking fossil evidence because no megaraptorans had been known from Europe until now. "These findings help to uncover the evolution of one of the most mysterious theropod groups," University College London doctoral student and study co-author Charlie Scherer said. The Invictibellatrix fossil, a fragmented braincase, was discovered about a century ago and acquired by the Natural History Museum in London in 1924. "It was left in one of the collection's drawers ever since, and no ⁠one noticed it until a couple of years ago," Scherer said. While Tyrannosaurus may be more imposing than Invictibellatrix, the researchers noted that if a person were somehow transported back in time — like in the recent film "The End of Oak Street" — Invictibellatrix might present more of a danger. "A smaller theropod like Invictibellatrix would likely have been a much bigger threat to a human than something like T. rex because ⁠we would likely be too small for T. rex to see as a worthwhile meal because of how massive it was and the amount of energy it would be required to catch us," Morrison said. "But we would be the perfect size for something smaller like Invictibellatrix, as we are about a third to a quarter of its weight, making us a good, hearty meal and more than just a snack. Additionally, Invictibellatrix would have the agility and manoeuvrability to pursue and catch a human." Copyright © 2026. Geo Television Network. All Rights Reserved.

title: Meta ordered to pay $25bn over FB privacy violations linked to Cambridge Analytica
description:
Published October 22, 2026 A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms to pay $25 billion on Wednesday after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that a political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign obtained data from ‌millions of Facebook users without their consent. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said it was one of the largest, if not the largest, single state verdicts against a company in American history. "Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict. Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion. In a statement, CJ Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal. “This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online." The company had previously said a penalty in the billions of dollars risked violating its constitutional rights to due process and protection from excessive fines. The penalty is the largest levied against the tech giant in the wake of the Cambridge Analytica scandal. In 2019, the company was hit with a $5 billion penalty by the US Federal Trade Commission stemming from the same scandal. Six other states settled their lawsuits related to Cambridge Analytica for $459.2 million as part of a $17.1 billion multistate settlement Meta reached in August to resolve states' claims that the company's platforms had harmed teen mental health. New Mexico's attorney general had sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app. The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data, how the company handles hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform and other internal policies. The company knew that third parties had broad access to users' personal data, and it tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company's bottom line, the state said. Cambridge Analytica, now defunct, worked for Trump's successful presidential campaign in 2016, and gained access to the personal information from millions of Facebook accounts for the purposes of voter profiling and targeting. It obtained that information without users' consent from a researcher who had been allowed by Facebook to deploy an app on its social media network. "It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable," Torrez told a press conference in Albuquerque after Wednesday's ruling. "I think today's judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers." Analyst Gil Luria, head of technology research at DA Davidson & Co, called the ruling costly but unlikely to impact the company's value. "Meta is worth nearly two trillion dollars, and will likely continue to appeal these cases and drag them out," Luria said.  Legal experts and financial analysts said the penalty was likely to face a lengthy battle on appeal. Jurors on September 25 found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading. They said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws, based on the number of Facebook users or New Mexico residents who were the audience for each misleading statement. State law allows a penalty of up to $5,000 per violation, and directs that all of the money go to New Mexico's school system, Torrez told reporters after the verdict. At a hearing on October 1, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, had asked Mathew to award the state between $35 billion and $40 billion, saying that would be supported by the US Constitution's protections on due process and the jury's verdict. "This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price," McGinn said. In court filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45 billion, saying a higher penalty ran the risk of scaring businesses out of the state. The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer had actually been misled, the company said in court filings. Daryl Lim, an associate dean at Penn State Dickinson Law, said that while the US Constitution generally protects against excessive fines, because of the way New Mexico law is written, the large size of the penalty does not automatically mean it could be overturned. The verdict was the second in six months by a Santa Fe jury in a lawsuit brought by the state of New Mexico against Meta Platforms. In the first trial, which ended in March, a Santa Fe jury ​found Meta misled users ⁠about young users’ safety on its Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp platforms and ordered the company to pay $375 million in civil penalties. After a second phase of that trial, a judge directed the company to pay $567 million into a New Mexico fund for teen mental health and ordered Meta to implement measures to protect teen Facebook and Instagram users in New Mexico. title: Websites go dark worldwide as AI exposes critical security flaws
description:
Published October 21, 2026 Government agencies and companies around the world shut down websites Wednesday after two critical flaws came to light involving PHP, a programming language that is the basis for a large share of the internet. The US National Security Agency told organisations to patch immediately or pull vulnerable systems offline. The flaws "often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," the NSA said in a statement on X. Attackers could use them to take over web servers without needing a password. PHP sits underneath popular web design platforms so the weaknesses potentially affect a vast range of websites, from online stores and news outlets to government services. The discovery came amid a surge in software security disclosures driven by increasingly powerful AI models, with the number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 on track to roughly double last year's record total. PHP volunteers released a fix on Wednesday. "If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now," the PHP Foundation, which funds developers working on the language, said in a blog post. The flaws were reported in August by security firm Calif and by ChatGPT maker OpenAI, which flagged them independently on the same day. Google-owned cloud security company Wiz later reported further ways to exploit them. The flaws had been reported privately to PHP's developers at the time and kept confidential while a fix was prepared. Details leaked online Tuesday, a day before the planned release, prompting the rush to take sites offline. In France, local government websites, including the Paris Police Prefecture, have been inaccessible since Wednesday afternoon at the request of the French National Cybersecurity Agency, following "detection of a critical security vulnerability," the Ministry of the Interior said. In the Netherlands, the national digital identity service DigiD, the website of the House of Representatives and the site of the national cybersecurity center went offline as a precaution, according to Dutch public broadcaster NOS. Belgium's foreign ministry temporarily took its websites offline as a precaution, it said on X, although the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium had recorded no attacks on Belgian sites. title: Hundreds queue in Hong Kong to glimpse Van Gogh painting unseen in public for 60 years
description:
Published October 13, 2026 Hundreds of people queued in Hong Kong on Tuesday to view a Vincent van Gogh painting never publicly exhibited in more than six decades, ahead of a Sotheby's ​auction in New York where it is expected to fetch about $180 million. The November 18 ‌auction will test the strength of the high-end art market, in which collectors have continued to compete for scarce trophy works, undeterred by broader economic uncertainty. Painted in May 1890, "Châtaigniers en fleurs", or "Chestnut Trees in Blossom", is one ​of the most important works from the Dutch artist's final days in the French ​village of Auvers-sur-Oise, where he died about two months later, aged 37. The painting ⁠is poised to set a new auction record for a Van Gogh work, said Scott Niichel, ​of Sotheby's modern and contemporary art department in New York. "This is a moment of extraordinary optimism, ​frenetic energy, enthusiasm, passion, and colour in the artist's body of work," he said. Paintings from Van Gogh's final Auvers-sur-Oise period, just after his release from a psychiatric asylum in Saint-Remy-de-Provence, rarely come to market, and the auction will ​draw the attention of collectors, museums and investors. "I'd never heard of this painting before, so I ​wanted to see it with my own eyes," said Li Shanshan, a 50-year-old art lover who travelled about ‌2-1/2 hours ⁠from the southern city of Shenzhen to view the artwork. The painting, which depicts a massive blossoming chestnut tree with a flowering canopy that dominates the composition, will be sold among part of a collection of 12 long-unseen works, including items by Paul Cezanne and Claude Monet. Five unveiled at Sotheby's ​in London in late ​September included Cezanne's "Arlequin" and ⁠Monet’s "Le Jardin des Tuileries". After Van Gogh's death in July 1890, "Châtaigniers en fleurs" was passed to his brother Theo, and then to the latter's widow ​Johanna van Gogh-Bonger and their son Vincent Willem. Subsequently, it was owned by ​German publisher ⁠Samuel Fischer, founder of S. Fischer Verlag, before entering the collection of George "Buddy" DeSylva, the American songwriter, film producer, and co-founder of Capitol Records.  Copyright © 2026. Geo Television Network.
